canonical_topic: Interest rate risk: forwards vs. futures cash flow timing
subcategory: Interest Rate Risk in Forwards vs Futures
definition: Forwards and futures differ in when their cash flows occur, which changes how exposed each is to interest rate risk.
core_idea: A forward contract settles with one large cash flow at the end of the contract, while a futures contract pays or collects small cash flows daily until maturity; because interest rate risk grows with the size and distance of a cash flow, the forward's single distant payment is far more rate-sensitive than the futures' stream of near-term payments.
key_points: Most energy trades occur in the future, so interest rates materially affect the profitability of those future cash flows.
For small notional amounts this effect can be immaterial; for large notional amounts it becomes a major source of risk.

Author's illustrative example: a 20-year contract to sell 500 MW of power, 7am-11pm, five days a week, to an industrial facility at an average price of $75/MWh represents a $3.1 billion exposure — showing the scale of cash flow at stake in a single large long-term power contract.
relationships: Builds on present value sensitivity to interest rate changes
Connects to earlier forwards-vs-futures distinction (not itself included in this chunk)
trading_implications: Long-dated forward-style power contracts carry meaningfully more interest rate risk than economically similar futures positions due to the timing of cash settlement.
Firms with large long-term forward exposures should treat interest rate moves as a real risk factor, not a rounding error.
